hints: Identify all four forces acting on the particle on the inclined plane: weight, normal reaction, applied force P, and friction F.

Ensure the directions are correct: weight acts vertically downwards, normal reaction acts perpendicular to the incline, P acts up the incline, and friction F acts up the incline to prevent sliding down.
walkthrough:
Draw a free-body diagram showing the particle on the $25^\circ$ inclined plane with four forces clearly indicated:
1. Weight $W = 12g$ acting vertically downwards.
2. Normal reaction $R$ acting perpendicular to the plane outwards.
3. Applied force $P$ acting up the plane parallel to the line of greatest slope.
4. Friction force $F$ acting up the plane parallel to the slope (opposing impending downward slide).
teacher_walkthrough: Sketch the inclined plane at an angle of $25^\circ$ to the horizontal and represent the $12\text{ kg}$ particle on the slope.

Indicate the four forces acting on the particle:
- Weight $W = mg = 12g\text{ N}$ acting vertically downwards through the center of mass.
- Normal reaction force $R$ acting perpendicular to the surface of the incline away from the plane.
- Applied pulling force $P$ directed upwards along the line of greatest slope.
- Friction force $F$ directed upwards along the plane parallel to the slope, opposing the tendency of the particle to slide down the plane.
Label all four forces with their names and show the $25^\circ$ angle clearly on the diagram.

hints: To find the least possible value of P, the particle is on the point of slipping down the plane, so limiting friction F acts up the plane.
Resolve forces perpendicular to the plane to find the normal reaction: $R = 12g\cos 25^\circ$.
Calculate the maximum available friction force: $F = \mu R = 0.35(120\cos 25^\circ)$.
Resolve parallel to the plane: $P + F = 12g\sin 25^\circ$, and solve for P.
walkthrough:
Resolve forces perpendicular to the plane in equilibrium with $m = 12\text{ kg}$ and $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$R = 12g\cos 25^\circ = 120\cos 25^\circ \approx 108.757\text{ N}$$

Calculate the limiting friction force acting up the plane (opposing impending downward motion):
$$F = \mu R = 0.35(120\cos 25^\circ) = 42\cos 25^\circ \approx 38.065\text{ N}$$

Resolve forces parallel to the plane in limiting equilibrium:
$$P + F = 12g\sin 25^\circ$$
$$P + 38.065 = 120\sin 25^\circ \approx 50.7142$$
$$P = 50.7142 - 38.065 = 12.6492\text{ N} \approx 12.6\text{ N}$$
teacher_walkthrough: State the physical condition for the least value of $P$: when $P$ is at its minimum, the particle is on the verge of sliding down the plane. Thus limiting friction $F = \mu R = 0.35R$ acts up the plane to help support the particle.

Resolve forces perpendicular to the $25^\circ$ inclined plane:
$$\sum F_\perp = 0$$
$$R - mg\cos 25^\circ = 0$$
$$R = mg\cos 25^\circ$$
Substitute $m = 12\text{ kg}$ and $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$R = (12)(10)\cos 25^\circ = 120\cos 25^\circ \approx 108.757\text{ N}$$

Compute the limiting friction force:
$$F = \mu R = 0.35(120\cos 25^\circ) = 42\cos 25^\circ \approx 38.0650\text{ N}$$

Resolve forces parallel to the plane:
$$\sum F_\parallel = 0$$
$$P + F - mg\sin 25^\circ = 0$$
$$P = mg\sin 25^\circ - F$$
Substitute the numerical values:
$$P = 120\sin 25^\circ - 38.0650$$
Compute $120\sin 25^\circ$:
$$120(0.422618) = 50.7142\text{ N}$$
Subtract the friction force:
$$P = 50.7142 - 38.0650 = 12.6492\text{ N}$$
Rounding to three significant figures gives:
$$P = 12.6\text{ N}$$
Thus the least possible value of $P$ to prevent sliding down is $12.6\text{ N}$.
